newsitem.title: TAIWAN: Taiwan shippers anxiously await China straits move.
newsitem.headline: Taiwan shippers anxiously await China straits move.

text.p: Taiwan shippers were casting an anxious eye towards Beijing on Monday, eager to know when or even if communist China would reciprocate a Taipei gesture and allow them to sail long-forbidden China-Taiwan routes.

Taiwan on Friday authorised four carriers from the rival mainland to sail directly to the Nationalist-ruled island with immediate effect -- gingerly easing a ban dating to the civil war that split them in 1949.

The move eliminated the final hurdle to the first direct sailings of the Taiwan strait in 48 years, although Taipei -- wary of Beijing's intentions -- has put restrictions in place forbidding direct cargo exchanges.
The move turned the focus to Beijing, where authorities have been reviewing applications from a dozen Taiwan shippers eager to ply direct routes across the Taiwan strait.
"We've been checking through the day with our mainland office but so far there's been no word," said an official at one major Taiwan carrier.
Other Taiwan shippers gave similar replies, with most asking for anonymity to avoid jeopardising their applications.
Uniglory Marine Corp, a Taiwan hopeful, said it had cancelled an April 25 celebration that would have hailed the first crossing, saying it was better to keep a low profile.
Officials reached in Beijing on Monday said they were working swiftly but that some applications had been found to be incomplete or their addresses unclear, causing some delays.
"We are trying our best to complete this approval process as quickly as possible," a foreign trade transport official in China's Ministry of Communications told Reuters.
"It will take time to organise the shipping certificates," the official said. "Our work is proceeding normally. We will do our best to hurry up."
Notice would be sent directly to approved Taiwan shipping firms and no announcement would be made, he added.

Direct sailings have far more political significance than economic, since Taiwan will allow mainland cargoes entering its southern Kaohsiung to be transshipped to third countries -- not to enter Taiwan customs.
Likewise, Taiwan cargoes cannot be put aboard vessels bound for mainland ports and still must transit via Hong Kong.
Taipei has banned direct links with the mainland since the Nationalist Republic of China, defeated by the communists in 1949, fled into exile on Taiwan.
International carriers are ineligible for the routes because Beijing, burnishing its view of Taiwan as a rebel-held province, regards Taiwan-mainland crossings as a domestic matter.
At the Taipei office of U.S. shipping giant Sea-Land Service Inc, general manager David Arsenault called the evolving cross-straits situation highly political -- and reversible.
"It's taken 40-plus years for this approval to come by but with the stroke of a pen it could be cancelled again," he said.
"There's nothing permanent about these political arrangements right now. Obviously the shipping industry is being used as a pawn in a very political game of chess," he said.

Arsenault said Sea-Land and other foreign carriers worried that the establishment of direct links could come at their expense, as Beijing has dictated that sailings be made by firms owned all or in part by interests in China, Taiwan or Hong Kong.
"That is something we are very concerned about, that we are not supportive of," Arsenault said.

Arsenault said the long-established "indirect" links under which mainland and Taiwan cargoes had been routed via Hong Kong had been open to all international carriers on an equal basis and that mainland-Taiwan routes also should be open to all.
